As part of Montclair's vendor security review for the pilot, the InfoSec team needs: 1) a network/topology diagram that shows segregation between control plane, inference pools, and tenant data paths; 2) evidence (logs/configs) that segmentation and egress controls are enforced in production; and 3) a short threat-model summary that maps realistic attacker paths and mitigations for the edge deployment option you offer.

For context: our reviewers are particularly concerned about tenant-to-tenant lateral movement, egress to SaaS data stores, and any shared sidecar components that handle KV caches. If you can include any evidence of red-team tabletop runs or simulation notes that's ideal.

Rajiv —

Appreciate the clear ask. I'm attaching a first-pass topology PDF (redwood_edge_topology_v2.pdf) and a short README that points at the evidence bundle we'll drop (segmentation-evidence-logs.zip). High-level notes up front:

- Topology summary: control plane (managed control plane in our region) is logically separated from tenant inference pools via VPC-level ACLs and dedicated subnets. Each inference pool runs in its own compute cluster with a sidecar proxy. Tenant requests are routed to tenant-specific worker groups; there is no host-level sharing of KV cache between tenants.
- Sidecars & KV cache: sidecars are per-node and enforce token-level tenant ACLs; we run an additional namespace isolation layer so cached KV buckets are tagged by tenant id and purged when worker ownership changes.
- Egress & bastioning: inference clusters do not have direct internet egress. Outbound flows go through an egress proxy / NAT fleet with allowlists per-tenant and per-route policies. Sensitive destinations (SaaS stores) require an explicit egress exception and are routed via a dedicated egress VPC with IP allowlist.
- Crypto and auth: TLS1.3 in transit, mTLS between internal components, KMS-backed DEKs for model artifacts (per-customer key wrapping available for Dedicated/Private).

Attachments included: redwood_edge_topology_v2.pdf (diagram, simplified IPs), evidence README (references logs we will deliver), and a placeholder attack-scenarios-runbook.md (draft). We'll follow up with the logs bundle and a short threat-model doc by Nov 9.

Before we proceed with sensitive artifacts: do you prefer that we redact internal IPs and account IDs in the diagrams (we can provide both redacted and full versions under an NDA)?

Rajiv / team —

Adding technical detail on the controls Ben summarized. This is intended to answer the "evidence" portion directly so your reviewers can map controls to requirements.

1) Network segmentation and enforcement - Per-cluster VPC/subnet separation: inference worker pools run in distinct subnets with route tables that prevent cross-pool routing except through approved service endpoints (control-plane API, egress proxies). - SGs and NACLs: security groups enforce least privilege by service account and port. NACLs used for an additional layer of deny-all-by-default. - Egress proxies: all outbound traffic exits via a managed egress fleet (controlled egress CIDR + proxy auth). We can provide proxy logs showing destination allowlist enforcement (see segmentation-evidence-logs.zip).

2) Identity & auth - mTLS between control plane and worker nodes; short-lived certs issued via our internal CA. - Token binding for tenant requests: tokens include tenant-scoped claims and are validated in the sidecar before any request touches the model or KV.

3) KV cache & sidecar attack surface - KV namespaces are tenant-tagged; access requires tenant token and node attestation. Cache mutation APIs are only accessible from internal runtime components, not user-facing APIs. - We run periodic cache-integrity checks (hashing / attestation) and have circuit-breaker policies that drop cache-serving capability if anomaly thresholds are hit. Evidence of a recent integrity check run is included in the logs bundle.

4) Data at rest & key management - All customer artifacts (model files, persisted caches) are encrypted at rest using KMS-managed keys. For Dedicated/Private customers we support customer-managed KMS/HSM integration; proof points are available on request.

5) Observability & audit - Comprehensive audit trail: token-level request logs, per-node process auditing, and end-to-end request traces (sample traces in logs zip). We retain audit logs in an immutable store for the period described in our SOC2 policy (retention windows configurable under enterprise agreements).

Attachments: segmentation-evidence-logs.zip (contains sample proxy logs, sample token validation traces, cache-integrity-run-2026-10-22.log).

If you want, Naomi can attach a redacted SOC2 evidence packet that maps controls to the AICPA criteria.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Director, Security Engineering
Redwood Inference

Rajiv —

Following up with a concise threat-model summary and notes from a tabletop attack simulation we ran internally against the edge deployment pattern. Attached: attack-scenarios-runbook.md (draft).

Executive summary:
- Attack surface highlights: compromised developer credentials -> supply chain/model artifact tampering; compromised sidecar process -> attempt to exfiltrate cached tokens/contents; misconfigured egress allowlist -> data egress to attacker-controlled endpoints.

High-risk paths and mitigations:
1) Sidecar compromise -> Lateral movement to worker process - Likelihood: low-to-medium (requires local code execution). - Mitigations: sidecars run with least privilege; runtime seccomp and process sandboxing; node attestation before sidecar is permitted to serve tenant traffic; token binding prevents use of stolen session tokens from other nodes.

2) KV cache poisoning / cache-based leakage - Likelihood: medium (if cache write APIs are exposed without strict checks). - Mitigations: cache mutation APIs accessible only to control-plane-signed requests; write operations require additional attestation and are rate-limited; cryptographic tagging of cached entries (signed metadata) prevents simple injection attacks. We also keep per-tenant cryptographic nonces to detect replay.

3) Egress exception misuse -> data exfiltration - Likelihood: low (policy enforcement at proxy + manual review gating). - Mitigations: per-tenant allowlists, human approval for persistent exceptions, automated data-loss detection at the proxy, and egress anomaly alerts tied into our incident response runbook.

Tabletop run notes (summary): we ran a short scenario simulating a compromised build artifact that attempted to leak model output via an outbound request. The sim triggered both cache-integrity checks and egress anomaly alerts; circuit-breaker policy isolated the worker pool and routed traffic to a reduced-capacity fallback model. We'll include the sim trace in the runbook attachment.

Recommendations for Montclair's review:
- If you require further assurance, we offer an optional on-site/remote penetration test that focuses on sidecar -> worker isolation and egress controls (we can coordinate scope and scheduling).
- We can produce a redacted diagram set that strips internal IPs and hostnames for public reviewers and provide a full set under NDA.
